title: Are India's Small Modular Reactors Worth ₹20,000 Crore?

content:
India's Small Modular Reactor plan is real, and it's not hype. It's also not the cheap clean energy fix some headlines suggest. The government has committed ₹20,000 crore to build five indigenous SMRs by 2033, and whether that investment makes sense depends on which question you're actually asking: are they cheaper than solar? No. Do they solve a problem solar can't? Yes.

Key Takeaways

  • SMRs are factory-built nuclear reactors up to 300 MW, about one-third the size of conventional plants, designed to go up faster and serve smaller grid zones.
  • India's first two SMRs (a 220 MW BSMR and a 55 MW unit) are planned for Tarapur, Maharashtra, targeting commissioning in 2033.
  • At roughly ₹64 crore per MW, SMRs cost far more to build than solar at around ₹5 crore per MW, but they provide round-the-clock power that solar alone can't.
  • Existing Indian nuclear plants charge about ₹3.83 per kWh. New SMRs will likely come in at ₹6 to 8 per kWh, still above solar's ₹3.10 per kWh.
  • The 2033 target is ambitious, but the BSMR-220 design draws on proven PHWR technology with its Detailed Project Report already approved.

What exactly is a small modular reactor?

An SMR generates up to 300 MW of electricity, about one-third the output of India's standard 700 MW PHWR plants. 'Modular' means its main components are made in a factory and shipped to the site for assembly, cutting construction time compared to building everything on-site from scratch.

BARC has three indigenous designs in development. The flagship is the BSMR-220, a 220 MWe pressurised water reactor with its Detailed Project Report already approved. The SMR-55 is a compact 55 MWe variant aimed at industrial clusters and remote applications. Both first units will be built at Tarapur in Maharashtra, which already holds nuclear site licences, cutting years off the regulatory approval process.

How much will India's SMRs actually cost?

Parliament was told that two 55 MW SMRs at Tarapur will cost ₹7,000 crore, working out to roughly ₹64 crore per MW. India's conventional 700 MW PHWR plants run about ₹23 crore per MW at current prices. Solar capacity sits at around ₹5 crore per MW to install.

FeatureSMR (first units)Traditional Nuclear (PHWR)Solar
Build cost per MW~₹64 crore~₹23 crore~₹5 crore
Construction time5-7 years10-15 years1-2 years
Generates power at nightYesYesNo
Electricity cost per kWh~₹6-8 (projected)~₹3.83~₹3.10-3.50

The cost premium comes from losing economies of scale that large plants benefit from, plus first-of-a-kind engineering costs that always inflate the price of a new reactor design. The same thing occured with wind turbines and solar cells, both of which cost far more per unit in their early commercial years before manufacturing scaled up.

The promise is that serial production will eventualy bring these costs down through the same mechanism. That's plausible, but no commercial SMR anywhere has yet proved it at scale.

Why build nuclear at all if solar is cheaper?

Because solar doesn't generate electricity at night or during monsoon cloud cover. Data centers and semiconductor plants need reliable 24/7 power. SMRs provide constant output with zero carbon emissions, filling a gap that renewables alone can't cover without expensive grid-scale storage.

Say you're running a semiconductor fabrication plant in Pune or a large data center in Hyderabad. You need power every hour of every day. A grid failure doesn't just slow production; at some facilities it can destroy a batch of chips worth crores. Grid batteries help, but at industrial scale they add significant cost and still can't cover outages lasting more than a few hours.

India's existing nuclear plants run at above 80 percent capacity factors year-round. That's what SMRs bring to smaller grids that can't justify a full 700 MW plant. The case for them isn't cheapness. It's reliability, and that's a different calculation entirely.

Is the 2033 target realistic?

Possibly, but not guaranteed. The BSMR-220 design is mature, its DPR is approved, and it draws on proven PHWR technology, reducing first-of-a-kind engineering risk. But Indian nuclear projects routinely slip by years. A 2033 commissioning is achievable; 2035 is the more conservative estimate worth planning for.

According to Nuclear Engineering International, the BARC road map envisions 60 to 72 months of construction after regulatory clearance. India's nuclear track record is less reassuring on that count: Kudankulam Unit 1 was planned for 2007 and came online in 2013. The Gorakhpur plant in Haryana broke ground in 1984 and is still incomplete.

The Tarapur SMRs have genuine advantages over those cases. The site is already licensed. The BSMR-220 draws directly on PHWR design with many components in serial domestic production. Private sector involvement is now permitted under the 2025 SHINE Act, which can accelerate capital access and project management. Still, anyone planning around the target date should keep a contingency ready, at least untill one of these units actually goes live and proves the timeline out.

Frequently asked questions

What is a small modular reactor in simple terms?

An SMR is a nuclear power plant scaled to under 300 MW, built from factory-made components and assembled on-site. India's flagship design, the BSMR-220, generates about 220 MW through nuclear fission, enough for a medium industrial zone. Its factory-build approach cuts construction time compared to a conventional plant.

Why is India building SMRs instead of just more solar panels?

Solar can't generate power at night or during cloud cover. Data centers and large factories need guaranteed 24/7 electricity. SMRs fill that gap with zero carbon emissions, unlike coal and gas that currently handle most of India's baseload power. Solar and nuclear are complementary, not competing.

Who is building India's small modular reactors?

BARC is developing the reactor designs. Tata Power has announced plans for India's first privately built nuclear plant by 2032. Adani Group and Reliance Industries have also signaled interest under the 2025 SHINE Act, which opened nuclear investment to the private sector for the first time in India.

How much will SMR electricity cost in India?

Exact tariffs haven't been set, but projections point to ₹6 to 8 per kWh for first-of-a-kind units, compared to ₹3.83 per kWh from existing nuclear plants and ₹3.10 to 3.50 per kWh from solar bids. Costs should fall as global and domestic production scales up over time.

Will India's SMRs be ready by 2033?

The government targets 60 to 72 months of construction after regulatory clearance. The BSMR-220 is the most likely to hit a 2033 date, drawing on proven PHWR technology with its DPR already approved. A slip to 2035 is plausible given India's nuclear history, but 2033 is achievable if approvals move smoothly.

How do India's SMRs compare globally?

China is ahead, with SMRs already under construction. The US, Canada, and the UK have active programs but no commissioned commercial units yet. India's plan is consistent with global momentum for next-generation nuclear. If BARC's designs prove reliable, India could eventually export reactor technology, a stated goal of the Nuclear Energy Mission.

The short version

India's SMR plan is not a vanity project. The reactors cost more per MW than solar and more per kWh than existing nuclear, but they deliver something renewables can't yet: guaranteed power at any hour, in any weather. The 2033 target is tight, though BSMR-220's proven PHWR foundations give it a real shot. The bigger question isn't whether SMRs make sense. They do. It's whether India can build them on time and drive costs down fast enough to justify the premium.
